The Jenyns sprat, Ramnogaster arcuata, is a small-bodied clupeiform fish endemic to the temperate freshwater and estuarine systems of southeastern South America. Field surveys utilising gill nets and trawls have established that the species attains a maximum recorded standard length of 12 cm [Li = 12 cm], placing it among the smaller members of the Clupeidae family. Individuals collected from the Río de la Plata basin consistently display rapid early growth, with length-frequency distributions suggesting that the majority of somatic expansion is completed within the first two years of life. During the austral spring spawning season, gravid females captured in the Paraná River delta were subjected to gonadosomatic analysis. The mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) for reproductive females was recorded at 9% [GSI = 9%] when assessed at the prevailing water temperature of 15.6 °C [T = 15.6 °C].

The onset of reproductive capability in Ramnogaster arcuata is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body size threshold. Examination of gonad histology from a size-graded series of specimens reveals that the standard length at puberty is 7.7 cm [Lp = 7.7 cm]. Individuals below this length consistently present immature, undifferentiated gonadal tissue, whereas nearly all fish exceeding this threshold display active gametogenesis or clear evidence of prior spawning. This length-based maturation schedule is broadly comparable to that documented in congeneric species from similar thermal regimes, supporting the view that size, rather than age per se, governs the timing of puberty in this lineage. The implications for population dynamics are substantial, as a relatively small size at maturity allows a greater proportion of the annual cohort to participate in reproduction, potentially enhancing the species’ resilience in the face of fluctuating environmental conditions within its estuarine habitats.

Early life history traits in Ramnogaster arcuata are inferred from closely related anchovy taxa due to the logistical challenges of rearing the delicate eggs under controlled laboratory conditions. Based on morphometric data from Engraulis anchoita, the estimated dry weight at birth of a newly hatched larva is approximately 0.0003 g [Wwb = approximately 0.0003 g], a value calculated from a mean egg length of 1.2 mm and a width of 0.7 mm using the standard prolate spheroid volume formula. This minuscule initial mass underscores the extreme vulnerability of the yolk-sac larva, which must rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for several days before the mouth opens and the onset of exogenous feeding becomes possible. Consequently, the density and spatiotemporal distribution of suitable planktonic prey items, such as copepod nauplii and rotifers, are likely critical determinants of first-feeding success and subsequent larval survival in natural systems.

Incubation dynamics and early developmental rates for this species are modelled primarily on the well-studied European anchovy, Engraulis encrasicolus, with which Ramnogaster arcuata shares a comparable reproductive ecology. At a stable incubation temperature of 15.7 °C [T = 15.7 °C], eggs are expected to complete embryogenesis and undergo eclosion after approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days]. The hatching event yields a small, transparent larva equipped with a prominent yolk sac that sustains the fish through its initial endotrophic phase. The duration of the yolk-sac larval stage is temperature-sensitive, and at the same thermal regime (15.7 °C [T = 15.7 °C]), the maximum lifespan for the species is estimated at roughly 5 years [am = roughly 5 years], a value consistent with the relatively short-lived, fast-paced life history strategy common among small, forage-fish clupeiforms. These temperature-dependent rates of development and mortality have direct consequences for the timing of cohort emergence relative to seasonal peaks in planktonic food availability.

Body mass at the terminal, fully grown stage in Ramnogaster arcuata has been estimated using a length-weight relationship derived from a large sample of adult specimens. The ultimate wet weight for Ramnogaster arcuata, calculated using a standard length-weight power function, yields a mean value of 16 g [Wwi = 16 g] at the species’ asymptotic standard length of 12 cm. The underlying allometric exponent, notably above 3, indicates a slight positive allometry in mass relative to length, meaning larger individuals are proportionately heavier-bodied than smaller conspecifics. Such a pattern may reflect an ontogenetic shift in body depth or condition factor as the fish matures and begins to invest more heavily in gonadal tissue and visceral fat reserves. In comparison to other members of the Clupeidae that inhabit similar South American river systems, Ramnogaster arcuata is neither particularly robust nor slender, occupying an intermediate position that aligns with its role as a mid-trophic-level planktivore.
